sentences.text: The Hubble Space Telescope has been changing our view of the universe since 1990.
It orbits at an altitude of 540 kilometers and, with its 2. 4-meter mirror, captures images free of the atmosphere's blur.
Its first images were blurry; a small flaw in its mirror was corrected in orbit by astronauts in 1993.
It measured the age of the universe, contributed to the discovery of dark energy, and with its Deep Field images showed thousands of galaxies in a spot of sky that appeared empty.
We begin this tour, on which we will visit humanity's ambassadors in space, from Earth orbit: before you is the International Space Station.
At an altitude of four hundred kilometers, it orbits at twenty-eight thousand kilometers an hour and completes a circuit of Earth in ninety minutes; here is that circuit, sped up.
Astronauts see sixteen sunrises a day.
It is the size of a football field and weighs four hundred and twenty tons.
Humans have lived aboard it continuously since November two thousand; this is humanity's longest continuous presence in space.

The James Webb Space Telescope orbits around Lagrange point 2, 1. 5 million kilometers from Earth on the side opposite the Sun. Its 6. 5-meter gold-coated mirror is made of 18 hexagonal segments, and it was folded up on Christmas 2021, when it was launched.
Because it sees in infrared light, it is cooled to minus 233 degrees by a sunshield the size of a tennis court.
It is studying the universe's first galaxies, the interiors of the dust clouds where stars are born, and the atmospheres of exoplanets.
New Horizons was the fastest spacecraft to leave Earth in 2006; it crossed the Moon's distance in 9 hours.
After a journey of 9. 5 years, it flew past Pluto in July 2015 and turned a blurry dot into a real world, with its mountains, glaciers, and heart.
Then in 2019 it visited snowman-shaped Arrokoth in the Kuiper Belt; this is the most distant object a spacecraft has studied.
It is still working and measuring the outer limits of the Solar System.
The Parker Solar Probe is the first spacecraft to touch the Sun.
It was launched in two thousand eighteen and, using Venus's gravity, tightened its orbit step by step; let's watch its orbit from above.

In December two thousand twenty-four it came within six million nine hundred thousand kilometers of the Sun's surface; at that moment, at six hundred and ninety thousand kilometers an hour, it became the fastest human-made object.
Its eleven-centimeter carbon shield withstands one thousand four hundred degrees, while the instruments behind it stay at room temperature.
Its purpose is to figure out why the Sun's outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface.
Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object.
It was launched in 1977; it visited Jupiter and Saturn, and gave up Pluto in order to approach Titan.
In 2012, by crossing the boundary of the solar wind, it became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space.
Today it is 25 billion kilometers away; its signals take more than 22 hours to reach us.
Aboard it is a golden record carrying greetings in 55 languages and the sounds of Earth: for someone who may find it one day.
And Voyager Two is the only spacecraft to visit all four outer planets.
It was launched sixteen days before its sibling, but on a slower route it flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
Most of what we know about Uranus and Neptune still comes from its flybys in nineteen eighty-six and eighty-nine.
In two thousand eighteen it reached interstellar space.
The plutonium batteries of both Voyagers are weakening; in the twenty-thirties they will fall silent, but for billions of years they will continue to glide among the stars; our tour ends here.
